payload.proof_nl:
Let A and B be finite sets, and assume |A| <= |B|. We must show that there exists an injective function f:A -> B.

Because A and B are finite, there exist nonnegative integers n and m such that |A| = n and |B| = m. The hypothesis gives n <= m.

Since A has exactly n elements, we may list its elements as
A = {a_1, ..., a_n}
if n > 0 (and if n = 0, then A = emptyset). Likewise, since B has exactly m elements, we may list distinct elements of B as
B = {b_1, ..., b_m}.

We now define f:A -> B.

Case 1: A = emptyset (equivalently n = 0).
Then there is exactly one function from emptyset to B, namely the empty function. It is injective vacuously, because there are no distinct x,y in emptyset. So the conclusion holds.

Case 2: n >= 1.
Define f on the listed elements of A by
f(a_i) = b_i for each i = 1, ..., n.
This is well-defined because n <= m, so b_1, ..., b_n all exist in B.

Also, f(x) is in B for every x in A, so f is indeed a function A -> B.

We now prove that f is injective. Let x,y in A and suppose f(x) = f(y). Since A = {a_1, ..., a_n} with distinct elements, there exist indices i,j in {1,...,n} such that x = a_i and y = a_j. Then
b_i = f(a_i) = f(x) = f(y) = f(a_j) = b_j.
But the elements b_1, ..., b_m are distinct, so b_i = b_j implies i = j. Hence x = a_i = a_j = y. Therefore f is injective.

Thus in all cases there exists an injective function f:A -> B. This proves the statement.

payload.statement_nl: Let A and B be finite sets. If |A| <= |B|, then there exists an injective function f:A -> B.

detailed_findings.finding: The proof gives a complete construction of the required injection for finite sets with |A| ≤ |B|.
The case split n=0 versus n≥1 is correct, and the injectivity argument is fully justified using distinct enumerations.
No semantic drift from the lemma sketch or the root theorem role is present; the lemma is exactly the standard finite-cardinality-to-injection fact needed downstream.

result_payload.reason: The proof correctly handles the empty-set case and the nonempty finite case by enumerating distinct elements of A and B, defining f(a_i)=b_i for i≤n, and proving injectivity from the distinctness of the enumeration of B. The argument matches the lemma statement and supports the root use of converting a cardinality inequality into an injection.
